question: What is the eponym for idiopathic sterile inflammation of the cavernous sinus?
explanation: Standardized tests have been known to ask easy questions and then list obscure eponyms for answers instead of descriptive disease names so it is a good idea to familiarize yourself with as many eponyms as possible. Wallenberg syndrome is also known as lateral medullary syndrome and is a constellations of findings (not all features necessary for diagnosis) associated with damage to the lateral medulla including an ipsilateral Horner's syndrome, ipsilateral loss of pain / temperature in the face, contralateral loss of pain / temperature in the body, and ipsilateral ataxia. Heimann-Bielschowsky phenomenon is a monocular vertical pendular nystagmus that occurs in poorly seeing eyes (often in children). It can occur following vision loss from low-grade pediatric optic nerve gliomas, amblyopia, trauma, and many other causes of vision loss. Because of the possibility of an optic nerve glioma, any child with monocular nystagmus (in clinic or on standardized tests) should have neuro-imaging performed if the cause of their vision loss has not already been elucidated in the past. Miller Fisher syndrome is an oculomotor predominant variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome that affects eye muscle movements first. After extraocular muscle involvement it can then progress to cause systemic motor and/or sensory neuropathy typical of Guillain-Barré syndrome. Tolosa-Hunt syndrome is idiopathic sterile inflammation of the cavernous sinus marked by severe ipsilateral periorbital pain along with deficits of any or all of the nerves passing through the affected cavernous sinus (CN 3,4,V1,V2,6 and the sympathetics). It is a diagnosis of exclusion after infectious causes of inflammation, lymphoma, and carcinoma have been excluded. Many patients who were previously given the diagnosis of Tolosa-Hunt are later found to have malignancies leading some experts to regard Tolosa-Hunt as a "waste basket" term used for other undiagnosed pathology. Which of the following diseases is NOT associated with agenesis of one or more cranial nerve nuclei in the brainstem? A.Congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles B.Superior oblique myokymia C.Duane syndrome D.Mobius syndrome High Yield: No Correct Answer: B Explanation: Congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles is thought to be caused by congenital agenesis of the 3rd nerve central levator palebrae superioris subnucleus and the bilateral 3rd nerve superior rectus subnuclei. Duane syndrome similarly is thought to be due to agenesis or dysgenesis of the 6th nerve nucleus and cranial nerve resulting in failure to abduct and/or adduct (depending on the subtype of Duane syndrome). Mobius syndrome occurs due to agenesis of the 6th and 7th cranial nerves producing failure of abduction bilaterally, esotropia, and facial diplegia. Superior oblique myokymia is an acquired disorder of irritation of the CN IV resulting in intermittent, high-frequency, low- amplitude contractions of the superior oblique muscle. The majority of these cases are idiopathic although very rarely there may be an inciting compressive lesion such as a neoplasm or vascular anomaly. There are no brainstem nuclei abnormalities associated with superior oblique myokymia. A 20-year-old female complains of intermittent binocular diplopia when she is reading late at night. Review of old photographs reveals a chronic right head tilt since early childhood. Alignment testing shows a left hypertropia that is worse on downgaze and right gaze. When testing each eye individually, eye movements appear full. When testing eye movements under binocular conditions there is a prominent up shoot of the left eye on far right gaze. Which of the following accurately describes her eye movement examination? A.Abnormal ductions and versions B.Normal ductions and versions C.Abnormal ductions with normal versions D.Normal ductions with abnormal versions High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: A good careful motility examination includes both ductions testing and versions testing. Ductions describe testing of ocular motility under monocular conditions (in other words, covering one eye and testing the other eye) while versions are tested under binocular conditions (both eyes open). Why does it matter? Sometimes, as in this case, a subtle motility deficit may not be appreciated under monocular ductions testing but is obvious when testing versions. In this case, the patient suffers from a classic case of a left congenital 4th nerve palsy with overaction of the inferior oblique. The inferior oblique "overaction" is a result of a weak antagonistic superior oblique muscle. The inferior oblique overaction effect is always most evident in adduction where the muscle has its greatest elevation effect. A 60-year-old woman presents with horizontal diplopia of recent onset. On exam, her visual acuity is 20/20 OU and her pupillary exam is normal. On testing of her versions, she appears to have no horizontal movement of her left eye and her right eye can only abduct. Her vertical gaze movements are normal. Her medical history is significant for a recent stroke. This patient's syndrome is most likely caused by a lesion of what structure? A.cerebellum B.midbrain C.pons D.thalamus High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: This patient displays the classic signs of one-and-a-half syndrome which combines the features of internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) with a ipsilateral gaze palsy. In this case, there is a LEFT one-and-a-half syndrome since there is impaired adduction OS (due to the left INO) as well as impaired abduction OS and impaired adduction OD (due to the left gaze palsy). The only horizontal eye movement remaining ("the half") is abduction of the RIGHT (contralateral) eye. This contralateral eye would classically display an abduction nystagmus as typically occurs in an INO. This syndrome is classically caused by a stroke or other lesion of the pontine region which contains the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) and paramedian pontine reticular formation (and CN VI nucleus). Vertical gaze is unaffected in this syndrome. As an aside, other interesting syndromes involving the MLF: • Raymond-Cestan syndrome: damage to MLF and corticospinal tracts; leads to INO + contralateral hemiparesis • "Eight-and-a-half syndrome": one-and-a-half syndrome + ipsilateral facial palsy (i.e. 1.5 + 7) Alternating hypertropia is a somewhat unusual but localizable finding marked by hypertropia alternating with hypotropia depending on gaze direction. An alternating hypertropia in which a right hypertropia is seen in right gaze and a left hypertropia is seen in left gaze indicates what diagnosis? A.Skew deviation B.Bilateral CN IV palsy C.unilateral complete CN III palsy D.Bilateral inferior rectus restriction High Yield: No Correct Answer: A Explanation: Skew deviation (SD) is admittedly confusing, but a few simple concepts will help clarify the entity. SD is a supranuclear disorder caused by a disruption of vestibular input (from the utricle and semicircular canals) to the brainstem nuclei responsible for vertical eye movement (CN III and IV). SD arises from either cerebellar or brainstem pathology but is difficult to more accurately localize. SD can result in comitant or incomitant vertical deviations which can complicate diagnosis. For unclear reasons, SD often manifests as weakness of the inferior rectus muscle(s). Skew deviation presenting with bilateral inferior rectus weakness presents with alternating hypertropia as detailed in the question, often localizes to the cervicomedullary junction, and can be associated with downbeat nystagmus. Alternating hypertropia can occur in bilateral CN IV palsies but in that case there would be hypertropia of the adducting eye (not abducting eye) so that there is a right hypertropia in left gaze and a left hypertropia in right gaze. This occurs because superior oblique weakness is most evident in the adducted position while inferior rectus weakness is most evident in the abducted position. CN III palsy (especially a partial CN III palsy with superior and inferior rectus weakness) can result in a hypertropia that alternates with up-gaze and down-gaze. With a partial right CN III palsy, for instance, there may be a left hypertropia on up-gaze and a right hypertropia on down-gaze. Bilateral inferior rectus restriction can occur with thyroid associated ophthalmopathy and would cause a left hypertropia on right gaze and a right hypertropia on left gaze. A 40-year-old female with Graves disease and confirmed thyroid-associated orbitopathy (TAO) suffers from binocular diplopia greatest on upgaze. Motility testing reveals a -2 upgaze deficiency in the right eye and a -1 upgaze deficiency in left eye. How could her particular case of strabismus be described? A.Paretic and comitant B.Paretic and incomitant C.Restrictive and comitant D.Restrictive and incomitant High Yield: No Correct Answer: D Explanation: Comitant strabismus is defined as strabismus where the degree of misalignment is equal in all gaze directions. Congenital strabismus is generally comitant in nature while paretic or restrictive strabismus is by definition incomitant. In this clinical scenario the patient has known TAO in which extraocular muscles become enlarged and fibrotic. Generally, the inferior rectus and medial rectus are the most commonly and worse affected muscles in TAO. The fibrotic changes in the muscle lead to a restrictive effect that prevents antagonist muscles from functioning properly. In this case, inferior rectus restriction prevents the superior rectus from elevating the eye properly. A lesion isolated to the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) in the pons or midbrain frequently results in which of the following? A.Skew deviation B.A contralateral gaze palsy C.Divergence insufficiency D.An up-gaze palsy High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Most people know that a lesion of the MLF causes an ipsilateral INO. You must also know, however, that a lesion of the MLF often causes a skew deviation in addition to an INO. Vestibular and cerebellar input (through the vestibular nuclei) project to the 3rd and 4th nerve nuclei to coordinate vertical gaze. This vestibular / cerebellar input also travels through the MLF (along with the interneurons connecting CN III and 6). A lesion of the MLF, therefore, often causes both INO and a skew deviation. In case you are unclear on the topic, a skew deviation is a vertical strabismus that can be comitant or incomitant. There are many different presentations of skew deviations but when caused by a MLF lesion, the hypertropic eye is USUALLY located on the side of the lesion. Some OQ customers in the past have been unsure of the meaning of "gaze palsy" leading to a wrong answer. A gaze palsy to one side means that BOTH eyes have limited motility to that side. For instance, a complete left gaze palsy means that the right eye is unable to adduct past midline and the left eye is unable to abduct past midline. A lesion of the CN6 nucleus or PPRF would be expected to cause an ipsilateral gaze palsy. A severe INO often causes an inability to adduct the eye on the same side as the lesion; the lack of adduction in one eye is NOT the same as a gaze palsy. A pupil-involving third nerve palsy is assumed to caused by an aneurysm until proven otherwise by neuro-imaging. Where is the most common location of the causative aneurysm? A.At the tip of the basilar artery B.At the junction of the basilar artery and the posterior cerebral artery C.In the posterior cerebral artery after the posterior communicating artery branches off D.At the junction of the posterior communicating artery and the internal carotid artery High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: D Explanation: One of the most feared and deadly neuro-ophthalmic emergencies, acute 3rd nerve palsy from aneurysm is frequently tested on standardized exams. While saccular aneurysms can occur virtually anywhere in the cerebral circulation, aneurysms at the junction of the posterior communicating artery and the internal carotid artery often present with a pupil involving 3rd nerve palsy by compressing the 3rd nerve as it passes by in the subarachnoid space. The parasympathetic fibers responsible for contraction of the pupillary sphincter muscle (and therefore miosis) travel in the peripheral segment of the nerve and are therefore very vulnerable to external compression. Microvascular 3rd nerve palsies can have pupil involvement but it is a diagnosis of exclusion made only after a thorough evaluation to rule out an aneurysm. question: A 60-year-old woman presents with horizontal diplopia of recent onset. On exam, her visual acuity is 20/20 OU and her pupillary exam is normal. On testing of her versions, she appears to have no horizontal movement of her left eye and her right eye can only abduct. Her vertical gaze movements are normal. Her medical history is significant for a recent stroke. This patient's syndrome is most likely caused by a lesion of what structure?
explanation: This patient displays the classic signs of one-and-a-half syndrome which combines the features of internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) with a ipsilateral gaze palsy. In this case, there is a LEFT one-and-a-half syndrome since there is impaired adduction OS (due to the left INO) as well as impaired abduction OS and impaired adduction OD (due to the left gaze palsy). The only horizontal eye movement remaining ("the half") is abduction of the RIGHT (contralateral) eye. This contralateral eye would classically display an abduction nystagmus as typically occurs in an INO. This syndrome is classically caused by a stroke or other lesion of the pontine region which contains the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) and paramedian pontine reticular formation (and CN VI nucleus). Vertical gaze is unaffected in this syndrome. As an aside, other interesting syndromes involving the MLF: • Raymond-Cestan syndrome: damage to MLF and corticospinal tracts; leads to INO + contralateral hemiparesis • "Eight-and-a-half syndrome": one-and-a-half syndrome + ipsilateral facial palsy (i.e. 1.5 + 7) Alternating hypertropia is a somewhat unusual but localizable finding marked by hypertropia alternating with hypotropia depending on gaze direction. An alternating hypertropia in which a right hypertropia is seen in right gaze and a left hypertropia is seen in left gaze indicates what diagnosis? A.Skew deviation B.Bilateral CN IV palsy C.unilateral complete CN III palsy D.Bilateral inferior rectus restriction High Yield: No Correct Answer: A Explanation: Skew deviation (SD) is admittedly confusing, but a few simple concepts will help clarify the entity. SD is a supranuclear disorder caused by a disruption of vestibular input (from the utricle and semicircular canals) to the brainstem nuclei responsible for vertical eye movement (CN III and IV). SD arises from either cerebellar or brainstem pathology but is difficult to more accurately localize. SD can result in comitant or incomitant vertical deviations which can complicate diagnosis. For unclear reasons, SD often manifests as weakness of the inferior rectus muscle(s). Skew deviation presenting with bilateral inferior rectus weakness presents with alternating hypertropia as detailed in the question, often localizes to the cervicomedullary junction, and can be associated with downbeat nystagmus. Alternating hypertropia can occur in bilateral CN IV palsies but in that case there would be hypertropia of the adducting eye (not abducting eye) so that there is a right hypertropia in left gaze and a left hypertropia in right gaze. This occurs because superior oblique weakness is most evident in the adducted position while inferior rectus weakness is most evident in the abducted position. CN III palsy (especially a partial CN III palsy with superior and inferior rectus weakness) can result in a hypertropia that alternates with up-gaze and down-gaze. With a partial right CN III palsy, for instance, there may be a left hypertropia on up-gaze and a right hypertropia on down-gaze. Bilateral inferior rectus restriction can occur with thyroid associated ophthalmopathy and would cause a left hypertropia on right gaze and a right hypertropia on left gaze. A 40-year-old female with Graves disease and confirmed thyroid-associated orbitopathy (TAO) suffers from binocular diplopia greatest on upgaze. Motility testing reveals a -2 upgaze deficiency in the right eye and a -1 upgaze deficiency in left eye. How could her particular case of strabismus be described? A.Paretic and comitant B.Paretic and incomitant C.Restrictive and comitant D.Restrictive and incomitant High Yield: No Correct Answer: D Explanation: Comitant strabismus is defined as strabismus where the degree of misalignment is equal in all gaze directions. Congenital strabismus is generally comitant in nature while paretic or restrictive strabismus is by definition incomitant. In this clinical scenario the patient has known TAO in which extraocular muscles become enlarged and fibrotic. Generally, the inferior rectus and medial rectus are the most commonly and worse affected muscles in TAO. The fibrotic changes in the muscle lead to a restrictive effect that prevents antagonist muscles from functioning properly. In this case, inferior rectus restriction prevents the superior rectus from elevating the eye properly. question: A pupil-involving third nerve palsy is assumed to caused by an aneurysm until proven otherwise by neuro-imaging. Where is the most common location of the causative aneurysm?

options.A: At the tip of the basilar artery
options.B: At the junction of the basilar artery and the posterior cerebral artery
options.C: In the posterior cerebral artery after the posterior communicating artery branches off
options.D: At the junction of the posterior communicating artery and the internal carotid artery

explanation: One of the most feared and deadly neuro-ophthalmic emergencies, acute 3rd nerve palsy from aneurysm is frequently tested on standardized exams. While saccular aneurysms can occur virtually anywhere in the cerebral circulation, aneurysms at the junction of the posterior communicating artery and the internal carotid artery often present with a pupil involving 3rd nerve palsy by compressing the 3rd nerve as it passes by in the subarachnoid space. The parasympathetic fibers responsible for contraction of the pupillary sphincter muscle (and therefore miosis) travel in the peripheral segment of the nerve and are therefore very vulnerable to external compression. Microvascular 3rd nerve palsies can have pupil involvement but it is a diagnosis of exclusion made only after a thorough evaluation to rule out an aneurysm. question: Which of the following would NOT be an expected finding in an isolated demyelinating lesion of the right medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) at the level of the rostral pons?

options.B: Impaired adduction of the left eye
options.C: Left beating nystagmus of the left eye on left gaze

explanation: Interneurons run from the 6th nerve nucleus in the mid- (as opposed to the ventral or dorsal) pons to the contralateral medial rectus subnucleus of the 3rd nerve in the rostral midbrain. This interneuron connection facilitates coordinated contraction of the medial and lateral recti to allow normal horizontal gaze. As these interneurons exit the 6th nerve nucleus, they immediately decussate to the other side of the brain stem and climb rostrally through the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) to the 3rd nerve medial rectus subnucleus. A lesion of the MLF disrupts coordination of the medial rectus and lateral rectus resulting in an internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO). A pontine lesion of the right MLF would be expected to cause a right INO with slowed adduction of the right eye, possible impairment of the motility of the right medial rectus (depending on the severity of the INO), and a possible left beating nystagmus of the left eye on left gaze. The MLF can be thought of as a conduit or highway for axons. In addition to interneurons connecting the 3rd and 6th nerve nuclei, the MLF also contains vestibular inputs to the brainstem nuclei affecting vertical eye movements. A lesion disrupting these pathways results in skew deviation. When present due to a lesion of the MLF, however, the side of the lesion typically corresponds to the hypertropic and incyclotorted eye. Skew deviation is very common in INO and is the first diagnosis that should come to mind when a patient with an INO has vertical binocular diplopia. For those wishing to better understand the complex topic of skew deviation, check out this excellent University of Iowa Eye Rounds case: http://www.eyerounds.org/cases/200-OTR.htm What distinguishes a lesion of the 3rd nerve nucleus from lesions of the 3rd nerve fasciculus or lesions of the 3rd cranial nerve (after exiting from the brainstem)? A.Bilaterality B.Involvement of the pupil C.Ipsilateral ptosis D.There are no distinguishing features High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Let's start by defining the 3rd nerve nucleus, fasciculus, and cranial nerve. The nucleus is located at the level of the rostral midbrain and is made up of the 3rd nerve neuronal cell bodies. These cell bodies give off a bundle of axons known as a fasciculus that pass inferiorly through the red nucleus and adjacent to the cerebral peduncle before exiting the brainstem as the 3rd cranial nerve. Lesions of different locations along this pathway (i.e. the nucleus, fasciculus, or cranial nerve) will manifest with different deficits clinically. A nuclear 3rd nerve lesion causes ptosis and ipsilateral mydriasis similar to a 3rd nerve fascicular or cranial nerve lesion. The distinguishing feature is involvement of the contralateral superior rectus and levator palpebrae superioris. Remember the 3rd nerve nucleus innervates the ipsilateral medial rectus, ipsilateral inferior rectus, and ipsilateral inferior oblique along with the contralateral superior rectus. The levator palpebrae superioris is innervated on both sides by a common central subnucleus. Due to the close proximity of the Edinger Westphall nucleus (housing the parasympathetic preganglionic cell bodies of the eye), the central levator palpebrae superioris subnucleus, and the 3rd nerve nucleus, a nuclear lesion often results in bilateral ptosis, bilateral superior rectus dysfunction, ipsilateral mydriasis, and ipsilateral dysfunction of the medial rectus, inferior rectus, and inferior oblique muscles. The superior rectus subnucleus of the 3rd nerve sends fibers to the contralateral superior rectus. The fibers of the superior rectus subnucleus, however, decussate very close to the contralateral 3rd nerve subnuclei. Due to this close proximity, a lesion causing a 3rd nerve nuclear palsy is clinically never truly isolated and virtually always involves the decussating fibers from the contralateral superior rectus subnucleus. Hypothetically, the perfect lesion could only affect one 3rd nerve nucleus without affecting the contralateral decussating superior rectus fibers but that is not seen in practice.

question: Which of the following is a possible treatment for the patient’s condition?

options.C: Bilateral loop myopexy between the superior and lateral rectus muscles

explanation: The patient has divergence insufficiency, which is defined as a mild-to-moderate esodeviation at distance with near motor fusion. The deviation is comitant and extraocular movements are usually full, although sometimes a small abduction deficit can be elicited. The condition is benign and patients typically have no other neurologic symptoms. Less commonly, divergence insufficiency may also be seen in association with other neurologic conditions such as Parkinson’s with concurrent nystagmus, tremor, and ataxia. Small, bilateral sixth nerve palsies may also mimic divergence insufficiency and neuroimaging is warranted in these cases. Otherwise, MRI imaging typically shows no abnormalities. There is a proposed, poorly-defined "divergence center" in the brainstem that has been attributed to the condition and may be disrupted in some patients, but this is currently debated. The most common known cause and proposed mechanism of divergence insufficiency in the elderly is sagging eye syndrome. This condition is caused by lateral and superior recti displacement inferiorly and nasally respectively due to degeneration of the connective tissue band that connects the two muscles. Infraplacement of the lateral recti causes the esodeviation. In some patients, the infraplacement can also lead to a small hypotropia and excyclotorsion of the affected eye. Patients are typically successfully treated with base-out prism or bilateral medial rectus recessions. WRONG ANSWERS: • Choice A: Refractive error correction alone would not correct the esodeviation. • Choice B: Base-in prism would correct an exodeviation, not an esodeviation. • Choice C: Heavy eye syndrome is seen in patients with axial high myopia, and therefore can be seen in younger patients. Patients present with an esotropia and hypotropia due to a supratemporal and posterior shift of the globe leading to medial displacement of the superior rectus and inferior displacement of the lateral rectus. Patients can have limited abduction and supraduction of the eye. This etiology of esodeviation should be differentiated from patients with sagging eye syndrome as medial rectus recessions can worsen the deviation. Instead bilateral loop myopexy of the affected muscles should be performed. MRI imaging can help differentiate if the clinician is uncertain. Which of the following diseases is not generally associated with restrictive strabismus? A.Skew deviation B.Thyroid associated orbitopathy C.Orbital myositis D.Orbital floor fractures High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Restrictive strabismus is always the result of damage to one or more extraocular muscles which prevent normal relaxation of the muscle. Damage can occur in the form of acute inflammation, entrapment, congenital maldevelopment or chronic inflammation with fibrosis. The two most common causes of restrictive strabismus are trauma (specifically medial and inferior orbital wall fractures) and extraocular muscle involvement associated with thyroid disease. Orbital myositis can cause a mixture of paretic and restrictive strabismus. Skew deviation is a vertical strabismus caused by disruption of vestibular input and/or cerebellar input to the brainstem nuclei responsible for vertical gaze (CN III and CN IV). There is no restrictive component in skew deviation. When cavernous sinus pathology results in one isolated cranial neuropathy, which nerve(s) is the most commonly affected? A.The abducens nerve B.The trochlear nerve C.The oculomotor nerve D.The third order sympathetic neurons High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Pathology of the cavernous sinus can often be localized by the involvement of multiple cranial nerves passing through the structure including cranial nerves 3, 4, V1, V2, 6, and the third order sympathetic neurons. When only one nerve is affected, the abducens is the most commonly affected because it passes relatively unprotected through the heart of the cavernous sinus while the other nerves are protected within the tough dural wall of the cavernous sinus (see answer image). Note that the image below is a coronal section of the right cavernous sinus. (Open source image: http://commons.wikimedia.org; many thanks to Brian Shapiro, M.D. for pointing out this image to us) What additional deficit would be expected in patients with a lesion that involves the right cranial nerve 6 nucleus? A.A right facial palsy B.A left gaze paralysis C.A right gaze preference D.An isolated abduction deficit in the right eye Topic: The Patient with Diplopia High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: A lesion of the right 6th nerve nucleus results in a right gaze paralysis meaning that the right eye does not abduct nor does the left eye adduct. This occurs because interneurons connect the right 6th nerve nucleus to the left medial rectus subnucleus (via the left medial longitudinal fasciculus) to allow coordinated horizontal gaze to the right. A lesion of the 6th nerve nucleus therefore causes more than simply an ipsilateral abduction deficit as would be expected with a peripheral 6th nerve lesion. The 6th nerve nucleus is located in the dorsal pons. The fascicle of the 7th nerve is also in the pons and essentially does a U-turn wrapping itself around the 6th nerve nucleus before exiting the brainstem at the cerebellopontine angle. For this reason, any lesion affecting the 6th nerve nucleus almost always causes an ipsilateral facial palsy. What is the cardinal feature (and most sensitive finding) of internuclear ophthalmoplegia? A.Slowed adducting saccadic velocity B.Abducting nystagmus C.Limited range of adduction D.Exotropia High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: All of the answer choices are findings of internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) but the only finding that MUST be present for the diagnosis is a slow adduction on the affected side as compared to abduction velocity of the contralateral eye. This may be the only finding in subtle or partially-resolved INO. By convention, laterality of INO is based on the eye with slowed adduction (i.e. a right INO results in lag of adduction in the right eye). A right INO may result in left beating nystagmus in the left eye when looking to the left (aka "abducting nystagmus"). A 10-year-old boy presents for evaluation of a lifelong eye movement problem. He has had bilateral ptosis and an inability to look up for his entire life. He maintains a large compensatory chin up head position. His vision is excellent (20/20 OU) and the remainder of his structural exam is unremarkable except for poor levator function in both eyes. Which of the following is NOT true regarding this condition? A.It is a form of congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles B.It is associated with agenesis of certain CN III subnuclei C.Surgical repair includes advancement of the levator aponeurosis for prominent ptosis D.It is often inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: C Explanation: This is a classic presentation of a type of congenital fibrosis syndrome known as congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles type I (CFEOM1) syndrome. The syndrome is similar to congenital ptosis in that there is congenital maldevelopment of the levator palpebrae superioris muscle leading to fibrosis of the affected muscles. In the case of CFEOM1, however, the process is bilateral and affects the superior recti muscles as well. Considering there is fibrosis of the levator palpebrae superioris, advancement or resection of the levator tendon will NOT be helpful. The general rule is that surgical intervention for ptosis with associated poor levator function requires a frontalis sling type procedure. Comparison of intraocular pressure (IOP) in primary gaze and upgaze is one means of diagnosing inferior rectus muscle restriction (in thyroid associated orbitopathy, for example). What threshold difference in IOP is considered significant? A.upgaze IOP 2 points higher than primary gaze B.upgaze IOP 5 points higher than primary gaze C.upgaze IOP 10 points higher than primary gaze D.upgaze IOP 15 points higher than primary gaze High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: Restriction strabismus is difficult to distinguish from paretic strabismus based on extraocular motility alone. Techniques to confirm restriction include forced duction testing with cotton swabs or forceps and the aforementioned comparison of IOP in primary gaze and gaze away from the restricted muscle. What percentage of "microvascular" or "vasculopathic" 3rd nerve palsies demonstrate some degree of pupil involvement? A.< 1% B.20% C.50% D.90% High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: B Explanation: Microvascular 3rd nerve palsies can have pupil involvement (~20% of cases) but it is a diagnosis of exclusion made only after a very thorough evaluation of the patient for a cerebral aneurysm using any combination of magnetic resonance angiography (MRA), computed tomography angiography (CTA), or conventional cerebral angiography. The precise definition of "pupil involvement" varies in the literature. As a practical rule in clinic, any anisocoria whatsoever is concerning and warrants a work-up while anisocoria greater than 2 mm is extremely concerning for a compressive mass of the 3rd nerve (most often an aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery (PCOM)). Put another way, pupil involvement of any degree raises concerns for a PCOM aneurysm but the suspicion increases with the amount of anisocoria. Ophthalmoplegic migraine most commonly presents in which patient population? A.Children B.Elderly patients C.African Americans D.Hispanics High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Ophthalmoplegic migraine is characterized by episodic, localized orbital pain or headache associated with partial or complete paralysis of the oculomotor nerve. It is a very rare cause of episodic 3rd nerve palsy and virtually always presents in childhood (although subsequent attacks can carry over into adulthood). The underlying etiology is unknown. Enhancement of the 3rd nerve on MRI and the intermittent nature of the attacks have led some to speculate that it is due to an undiagnosed focal inflammatory lesion such as a sarcoidosis or lymphoma. Some have speculated that these regions of enhancement represent schwannomas although skeptics point out that schwannomas usually cause progressive nerve weakness rather than the waxing and waning nature typical of ophthalmoplegic migraine. In general, ophthalmoplegic migraine remains a diagnosis of exclusion after other more sinister pathology such as lymphoma, leukemia, and infectious disorders have been ruled out by a spinal tap and/or systemic work-up. Which nucleus innervates the left superior rectus muscle and which nucleus innervates the left superior oblique muscle (respectively)? A.The right 3rd nerve nucleus; the right 4th nerve nucleus B.The left 3rd nerve nucleus; the left 4th nerve nucleus C.The right 3rd nerve nucleus; the left 4th nerve nucleus D.The left 3rd nerve nucleus; the right 4th nerve nucleus High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: You must memorize the basic anatomy of the brainstem. The right 3rd nerve nucleus innervates the right inferior oblique (IO), right inferior rectus (IR), right medial rectus (MR), and LEFT superior rectus (SR). The levator palpebrae superioris (LPS) muscles on both sides are innervated by a centrally located common 3rd nerve subnucleus. This anatomy is very clinically relevant because a lesion of the 3rd nerve nucleus presents in a characteristic fashion with a classic ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy (from involvement of the ipsilateral IR, IO, SR, MR, and LPS) in addition to a contralateral palsy of the superior rectus and levator palpebrae superioris. Based on the anatomy, maybe you are wondering why lesions of the 3rd nerve nucleus also affect the ipsilateral superior rectus considering it is innervated by the contralateral 3rd nerve nucleus. This occurs because fibers from the superior rectus subnucleus decussate and pass adjacent to the contralateral 3rd nerve nucleus. Therefore, virtually all lesions affecting the 3rd nerve nucleus will also hit fibers from the contralateral superior rectus subnucleus as they pass by in the brainstem. The 4th nerve nucleus travels dorsally and is the only cranial nerve to exit along the dorsal aspect of the brainstem. Before exiting, the 4th nerve fasciculus decussates so that the left superior oblique muscle is actually innervated by the right 4th nerve nucleus.

question: What percentage of "microvascular" or "vasculopathic" 3rd nerve palsies demonstrate some degree of pupil involvement?
explanation: Microvascular 3rd nerve palsies can have pupil involvement (~20% of cases) but it is a diagnosis of exclusion made only after a very thorough evaluation of the patient for a cerebral aneurysm using any combination of magnetic resonance angiography (MRA), computed tomography angiography (CTA), or conventional cerebral angiography. The precise definition of "pupil involvement" varies in the literature. As a practical rule in clinic, any anisocoria whatsoever is concerning and warrants a work-up while anisocoria greater than 2 mm is extremely concerning for a compressive mass of the 3rd nerve (most often an aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery (PCOM)). Put another way, pupil involvement of any degree raises concerns for a PCOM aneurysm but the suspicion increases with the amount of anisocoria. Ophthalmoplegic migraine most commonly presents in which patient population? A.Children B.Elderly patients C.African Americans D.Hispanics High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: Ophthalmoplegic migraine is characterized by episodic, localized orbital pain or headache associated with partial or complete paralysis of the oculomotor nerve. It is a very rare cause of episodic 3rd nerve palsy and virtually always presents in childhood (although subsequent attacks can carry over into adulthood). The underlying etiology is unknown. Enhancement of the 3rd nerve on MRI and the intermittent nature of the attacks have led some to speculate that it is due to an undiagnosed focal inflammatory lesion such as a sarcoidosis or lymphoma. question: Non-invasive angiography such as magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) and computed tomography angiography (CTA) are frequently used to assess for posterior communicating artery aneurysms in cases of third nerve palsies. These tests can reliably detect aneurysms as small as what size?
explanation: The gold standard for cerebral aneurysm detection has been and remains invasive catheter angiography. With the advent of more sophisticated neuro-imaging providing better definition, however, CTA and MRA are now capable of detecting virtually all aneurysms large enough to cause a 3rd nerve palsy. Recent studies have shown that the vast majority of aneurysms missed by CTA or MRA are actually the result of a missed finding on radiologic interpretation. In other words, evidence suggests that most false negatives in these cases are a result of human error rather than an intrinsic limitation of the MRA or CTA study. What is the primary clinical feature that aides in distinguishing a lesion of the cavernous sinus from a lesion of the orbital apex? A.The presence or absence of optic nerve involvement B.The presence or absence of involvement of the superior division of CN3 (without inferior division) C.The presence or absence of V1 involvement D.The presence or absence of the sympathetic nerves High Yield: Yes Correct Answer: A Explanation: The cavernous sinus and the orbital apex share many of the same nerve components including cranial nerves 3, 4, V1, and 6 along with third order sympathetic neurons. Often times exam features are not sufficient to distinguish between pathology of the orbital apex and cavernous sinus in which case localization must rely on neuro-imaging. In these tricky situations, an optic neuropathy does definitively localize the process to the orbital apex. The optic nerve does not pass through the cavernous sinus. Keep in mind that the same process in theory could also extend posteriorly to involve the cavernous sinus. The oculomotor nerve divides into its superior and inferior divisions in the anterior cavernous sinus before both divisions pass through the orbital apex; for this reason a divisional 3rd nerve palsy is not helpful in distinguishing between orbital apex and cavernous sinus lesions.
